name: Webster Square
headline: The old New Worcester crossroads,
where Stafford Street leaves Main Street for Leicester.
answer: Webster Square is a South Worcester neighborhood that grew around the junction of Main, Mill, Webster and Cambridge Streets, the mill village once called New Worcester. Loring and Aury Coes built their wrench and knife works here, and Coes Reservoir and its parks lie along Mill Street. Stafford Street begins at the square, Route 12 crosses it on Mill Street, and WRTA Route 19 runs from Webster Square to Clark University on Main Street.
meta: Webster Square, Worcester: the old New Worcester crossroads, the Coes wrench works, Coes Pond parks, Stearns Tavern and WRTA Route 19. A sourced neighborhood guide.

boundaries.text: Webster Square first meant the junction of Main, Mill, Webster and Cambridge Streets in southwestern Worcester; the name now covers the neighborhood west of that junction along Main Street, toward the intersection of Main Street, Park Avenue and Stafford Street, about 0.7 miles farther west. Wikipedia's list of Worcester neighborhoods places Webster Square in South Worcester.

overview: Webster Square began as a mill village on Kettle Brook. The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Worcester records the first water-powered spinning of cotton yarn in the town at Trowbridgeville, or New Worcester, at Joshua Hale's mill on Kettle Brook, and a federal report of 1832 listed two satinet mills on Curtis Pond near Webster Square. Roads met here early: the Holland, Worcester and Stafford Turnpike (Stafford Street), which gave a direct route to the southwest after 1810, began at Main Street at New Worcester, and by 1830 a small residential cluster stood at Webster Square on Main Street. Charles Stearns opened a tavern on Main Street in 1812; its building, dated to about 1812, still stands. Phineas Ball's 1860 city map labels the area New Worcester, and Samuel Triscott's 1878 map uses the name Webster Square.

Industry and the street railway built the square out. Loring Coes, born at New Worcester in 1812, patented a screw wrench in 1841, and with his brother Aury and Levi Hardy bought Moses Clement's shop at the corner of Main and Mill Streets in 1853. In 1865 to 1867 the Coes brothers and Hardy bought 100 acres of the Lyon Farm, now the site of Coes Pond, and built a dam and a knife shop there, followed by a lower dam at Coes Square in 1867 and a four-story wrench factory at Coes Square in 1871. Worcester's first horsecar line, opened in 1863, ran from Webster Square through downtown to Bell Hill, and the 1916 streetcar route list still included lines from Webster Square to Barber's Crossing, Union Station and Lincoln Square. A walking history of the road notes that most of the lots along Main Street west of the square were developed with three-deckers.

The square is now a busy crossroads. Route 12 crosses it on Mill Street before joining Route 9 on Park Avenue, and Webster Square Plaza, a late-twentieth-century shopping plaza, fills the large lot between Main Street and Stafford Street. The Worcester Housing Authority owns Webster Square Towers East and West at 1050 and 1060 Main Street and, in 2002, bought the former Webster Square Cinemas building at 24 Mill Street; after selling it in 2004, it bought it back for its maintenance and property management offices. Up Mill Street, the city's Coes Pond parks cover about 21 acres around Coes Reservoir, including Coes Park on the former Coes Knife factory site, where the Stearns Tavern building was moved in October 2016.

housing.text: A walking history of the Main Street corridor notes that most of the lots west of the square were developed with three-deckers, alongside substantial two-family houses such as the six at 1286 to 1296 Main Street, and that the footprint of Webster Square Plaza hides how residential the area was first built. Webster Square Towers East and West, at 1050 and 1060 Main Street, are Worcester Housing Authority buildings. No published count of housing types or ownership for Webster Square alone was found.

areas.name: The square: Main, Mill, Webster and Cambridge Streets
areas.line: The original junction, with the Webster Square fire station at 40 Webster Street and the Worcester Housing Authority's Webster Square Towers at 1050 and 1060 Main Street.

areas.name: Main Street west to Park Avenue and Stafford Street
areas.line: Main Street climbs west from the square toward Leicester past Webster Square Plaza, which fills the lot between Main and Stafford Streets, three-deckers and two-family houses, and Our Lady of the Angels Church at 1222 Main Street.

areas.name: Mill Street and Coes Pond
areas.line: The Coes industrial district: the dams and wrench factory at Coes Square, Coes Reservoir and its parks, the Stearns Tavern building at 140 Mill Street, and the Major Taylor Bike Trail along Mill Street.

commute.text: Webster Square has no rail station; the nearest is Worcester station at Union Station, 2 Washington Square, downtown, on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. Route 12 runs north on Webster Street past Hope Cemetery, crosses Webster Square as Mill Street and joins Route 9 on Park Avenue. WRTA Route 19 runs from Webster Square to Clark University via Main Street, and Route 825 is the Park Avenue Connector.

places.name: Coes Park
places.line: A city park at 72 Coes Street on the former Coes Knife factory site, with a universally accessible playground of 57 features, a sledding hill, a scenic overlook and ADA-accessible walkways on Coes Reservoir, commonly called Coes Pond.

places.name: Stearns Tavern
places.line: A tavern building dated to about 1812, moved from 1030 Main Street to 651 Park Avenue in 1974 and to 140 Mill Street in October 2016; the Seven Hills Foundation uses its first floor for a cafe and workforce training.

places.name: Binienda Beach
places.line: The swimming beach on the western side of Coes Reservoir, formerly Coes Pond Beach, named for the late State Representative John J. Binienda, with a bathhouse and seasonal kayak, paddle boat and paddle board rentals.

places.name: Columbus Park
places.line: The park on the eastern side of Coes Reservoir, kept largely natural by its steep slopes, with a small beach in its southwest corner.

places.name: Major Taylor Bike Trail
places.line: A bike trail along Mill Street past Coes Pond and the former Coes Knife property, named for Marshall Walter 'Major' Taylor, who won national and world bicycle sprint championships in 1899.

places.name: Hope Cemetery
places.line: A 168-acre garden cemetery at 119 Webster Street, on land an 1851 mayoral report placed south of New Worcester; Loring Coes was one of its five original commissioners, and it was listed on the National Register in 1997.

places.name: Our Lady of the Angels Church
places.line: A Catholic church at 1222 Main Street; the parish was founded in 1916 and the present building opened in 1927.

history.text: The Holland, Worcester and Stafford Turnpike (Stafford Street) opened a direct route to the southwest, beginning at Main Street at New Worcester, later Webster Square.
Worcester's first horsecar line opened, running from Webster Square through downtown to Bell Hill via Main and Lincoln Streets.
Loring Coes built a four-story wrench factory at Coes Square, four years after the lower dam there.
The Stearns Tavern building was moved in October from Park Avenue to 140 Mill Street, on the former Coes Knife site.

search_notes: A search for 'Webster Square Worcester MA real estate' returned only Redfin's Webster Square neighborhood listing pages (recently sold, new listings, filtered views); other research searches returned Walk Score, zipdatamaps, Apartments.com unit listings and the Boston Rambles walking history. Wikipedia has no Webster Square article. No sourced guide ties the New Worcester mill village, the Coes works, the 1863 horsecar line and today's Coes Pond parks together, which is the gap this page fills.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Webster Square, Worcester?
faq.a: The Warren Group does not report Webster Square separately. Citywide, the median single-family sale price in Worcester for calendar year 2025 was $430,000 across 884 sales, up from $420,000 across 904 sales in 2024, according to its MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report.

faq.q: Is there commuter rail near Webster Square?
faq.a: Webster Square has no station of its own. The nearest is Worcester station at Union Station, 2 Washington Square, downtown, on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. WRTA Route 19 runs from Webster Square to Clark University along Main Street.

faq.q: Which school district serves Webster Square?
faq.a: Worcester Public Schools. School assignment is by address and is set by the district; review the district's profile with DESE.

The name first meant the junction of Main, Mill, Webster and Cambridge Streets in southwestern Worcester, an area once called New Worcester. It now covers the neighborhood west of that junction along Main Street toward Park Avenue and Stafford Street.

faq.q: Is Coes Pond in Webster Square?
faq.a: Coes Reservoir, commonly called Coes Pond, lies along Mill Street, which runs through the square. The Coes brothers built their knife shop and dams there in the 1860s, and the city's Coes Pond parks, about 21 acres, now include Coes Park, Binienda Beach and Columbus Park.

notes: Written 2026-10-23. Boundaries: no official city boundary was found. The Boston Rambles walking history (an independent blog, used for local geography and some dates) says Webster Square 'once referred to the intersection of Main, Webster, and Cambridge Streets' and 'has long since become a name for the entire neighborhood west of the intersection'; it calls the junction that of 'Main Street, Mill Street, Webster Street, and Cambridge Street' and places the Main/Park/Stafford intersection about 0.7 miles farther west, where a plaque names it Gardner Square. The task brief placed Webster Square at Main Street and Park Avenue; on these sources the square proper is the Main/Mill/Webster/Cambridge junction, and Park Avenue meets Main and Stafford Streets to its west. The city's April 22, 2024 Stafford Street meeting notice (https://worcesterma.gov/calendar/stafford-street-informational-meeting) describes 'Stafford Street between Webster Square and the Leicester Town Line', and the MHC report says the Stafford Turnpike began 'at Main Street at New Worcester (later Webster Square)'. Wikipedia's neighborhood list (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_in_Worcester,_Massachusetts) places Webster Square in South Worcester. Name: the blog cites Ball's 1860 map ('New Worcester') and Triscott's 1878 map, which it treats as the first naming of Webster Square; but the MHC report lists a 'Webster Square (1860)' church in its Early Industrial period, so no first-use date is claimed. The Worcester Historical Museum finding aid says Loring Coes 'was born at Webster Square (then called New Worcester)'. Why the square is named Webster was not found. Coes dates: the overview follows the Worcester Historical Museum finding aid for the Coes family papers (1853 purchase with Levi Hardy; 1865-67 Lyon Farm, dam and knife shop; 1867 lower dam at Coes Square; 1871 wrench factory; 1902 merger into the Coes Wrench Company). Wikipedia's Coes Wrench Company article says that company was founded April 1, 1888 and merged with Loring Coes & Company in 1888; the merger date is left out because the sources conflict. The patent date (April 16, 1841) is from Wikipedia's Loring Coes article; the UMass Chan history page says 1840. Stearns Tavern: Wikipedia dates the building c. 1812 and gives the 1974 and 2016 moves; the 1812 opening by Charles Stearns is from Caleb Wall's Reminiscences of Worcester (1877) as quoted by the blog, which also argues the original tavern stood at 1050 Main Street rather than in this building, so the record says only that the building is dated to about 1812. The tavern was removed from the National Register on December 26, 2023 (after its move). The city calls it '204-year-old', which matches c. 1812 at the time the page was written; not repeated. Coes Pond acreage: the city page gives 20.79 acres in its introduction and 23.2 acres in Quick Facts; 'about 21 acres' follows the introduction. The city page also calls the reservoir the headwaters of the Blackstone River; not repeated. Webster Square Towers: the Worcester Business Journal article on the WHA's repurchase of 24 Mill Street (https://wbjournal.com/article/worcester-housing-authority-buys-back-improved-webster-square-property) describes the towers' tenancy; not used (it describes who lives there). Tower addresses 1050 and 1060 Main Street are from city police calendar notices (https://www.worcesterma.gov/node/47044, https://www.worcesterma.gov/node/48357) and the blog. The WBJ article gives no publication date, so the year of the repurchase is not stated. Webster Square Plaza is described only as the blog describes it ('a late-twentieth-century addition'); no tenants or business details. Fire station: the city lists the 'Webster Square' station at 40 Webster Street; Wikipedia's Webster Street Firehouse article says the 1893 E. Boyden & Son firehouse there was demolished around 2000 and replaced. Hope Cemetery: the Friends of Hope Cemetery tour map says it was dedicated in 1852 and placed on the National Register in 1998; Wikipedia says founded 1854 and listed December 22, 1997 (the NRHP list agrees: 97001560); the record gives 1997 and no founding year. Our Lady of the Angels: address confirmed by the city's Stafford Street meeting notice; the 1916 and 1927 dates are from the blog only. WRTA: route names from https://www.therta.com/routes/ (Route 19 'Webster Square - Clark University via Main St.'; Route 825 'Park Avenue Connector'); Route 27 (Auburn Mall via Main St.) and Route 7 (via Mill St.) were not confirmed to pass the square and are left out. Route 12 and Route 9 wording is from Wikipedia's Route 12 article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_12). Left out: the Cambridge Street School and Cambridge Street Firehouse (Cambridge Street is listed as a separate South Worcester neighborhood); Beaver Brook Park (300 Chandler Street, no source places it in Webster Square); Lakeside Apartments; the 1851 report's and the city's 'densely populated residential neighborhoods' wording; the Seven Hills Foundation's program participants. Market null: the Warren Group PDF lists Worcester only as a citywide row (read this session: 'YTD Number of Sales 904 884 -2.2%'; 'YTD Median Sale Price $420,000 $430,000 2.4%'); it does not list Webster Square (its 'WEBSTER' row is the Town of Webster). No population figure: no source gives one for this boundary. School assignment is by address and set by the district. Fair housing: no wording describes residents; the blog's and WBJ's descriptions of who lived or lives in the area were not used.
